rationale: ADHD-200 site effects (scanner, TR, protocol) are large and likely swamp the subtle ADHD connectivity signal. Scoring is within-site, so I'll standardize each connectivity feature per site before the L2 logistic regression. Each feature is centered and scaled using the training subjects from the same site, which removes site offsets and lets the classifier learn only within-site differences. This uses no labels, and site is used only to harmonize, never as a predictor.

In fMRI connectome benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019), tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk covariances is consistently the strongest connectivity measure. It captures how each subject deviates from a group reference covariance, which is more informative than raw Pearson correlations, especially when scans are short and noisy as they are at several ADHD-200 sites. This round I swap the Pearson features for tangent-space features on the same CC200 atlas and keep the same classifier. The reference mean is fitted only on the training fold.

Use the same tangent-space plus logistic-regression pipeline on several parcellations (CC200, AAL, HO, TT) and average their decision functions. Each atlas divides the brain differently, so its errors should be partly independent, and averaging them should lower the variance of the weak ADHD signal. In the Dadi et al. benchmarks, ensembles across atlases did reliably better than any single atlas.

I'm adding Riemannian re-centring per site. Each subject's covariance is whitened by the Riemannian mean of the training covariances from the same site, and the tangent space is then taken at the identity. Round 1's per-site z-scoring of Pearson features hurt; this keeps the geometry and removes scanner/protocol-specific covariance structure, leaving within-site deviations, which is what the within-site AUROC scores. The site references use only training-fold, label-free data, and any unseen site falls back to the global training mean.

Correlation matrices throw away each region's fluctuation amplitude, and ALFF differences are among the most replicated rs-fMRI findings in ADHD. This round I embed Ledoit-Wolf covariance matrices in tangent space instead. Before that, each subject's time series is divided by their median regional SD, which keeps relative regional amplitude (an ALFF/fALFF-like measure) and removes subject-, site- and scanner-wide scaling.

The L2 strength (C=0.001) was set by hand. With p≈20k tangent features, n≈700 and a weak, site-confounded ADHD signal, the right amount of shrinkage matters a lot. This round I pick C from a small grid using inner grouped CV on the training fold only, scored with the same within-site AUROC as the harness. Instead of predicting from a single C, I average the predicted probabilities of the two best C values to lower the variance of the selection.

ADD prevalence differs a lot between ADHD-200 sites, and site effects are large. So the global classifier can fit labels using site-specific connectivity directions, which does nothing for within-site AUROC. This round I keep the tangent-space and LR pipeline and reweight the training subjects so that ADHD and controls carry equal total weight inside each site, with each site's total weight kept proportional to its size. That makes the label statistically independent of site during training, so the model has to learn within-site connectivity differences. Unlike rounds 1 and 4, the features are left untouched.

I'm switching from the CC200 parcellation to the finer CC400 one (~392 ROIs) and keeping the same LW → tangent-space → logistic-regression pipeline. Round 3 suggests the coarse anatomical atlases were dragging the average down, and ADHD connectivity effects are thought to be small and local (striatal, thalamic, cerebellar), which finer data-driven parcels may resolve better. Because tangent features grow about 4× (from about 20k to about 77k) and the logistic-regression score's variance grows with feature count, I rescale C by 20100/p to keep the same effective regularization. This works out to C=0.001 at CC200.

ADHD-200 scans are short and noisy, so with about 20k tangent features and a few hundred subjects the classifier mostly fits within-subject sampling noise. This round I add time-crop augmentation to training only. Each training subject adds two extra Ledoit-Wolf correlation matrices, one from each half of its scan, alongside the full-scan matrix, weighted so each subject still totals 1. This should teach the logistic regression connectivity directions that hold up under resampling noise. The tangent reference, the scaler and the test predictions still use only the full-scan matrices.

Per-feature z-scoring of the ~20k tangent coordinates gives low-variance coordinates the same weight as high-variance ones. These include noisy edges of low-SNR or partly out-of-FOV ROIs and near-constant diagonal terms, and z-scoring amplifies their noise. It also distorts the Riemannian geometry that makes the tangent embedding work. This round I centre the features on the training mean and divide by a single global scale (the RMS of the training SDs), so the effective regularization stays close to the current one and the tangent-space geometry is preserved.

Some subjects have cc200 ROIs that fall outside the field of view, and right now those get identity rows and columns. In tangent space that is a large artificial deviation from the reference, and because the reference whitening mixes all ROIs, it contaminates every coordinate for that subject, not just the dead ROI's edges. This change fills in each dead ROI using only training-fold information, as the expected covariance given the subject's good ROIs. The fill-in is computed from the training population's correlation matrix, uses no labels, and keeps every matrix positive-definite. Tangent-space embedding then sees only real connectivity deviations.

Converting each region's signal to a correlation matrix throws away regional fluctuation amplitude (ALFF-like), one of the more replicated rs-fMRI findings in ADHD. Round 5 put amplitude inside the covariance, which changed the whole tangent geometry and lowered the score. This round leaves the connectivity model untouched and adds a separate, strongly regularised logistic regression on per-ROI log-SD of the time series. Each subject's log-SDs are made relative by subtracting their own median, which removes scanner/site gain. The two models are combined by adding their logits, i.e. treating them as independent evidence, so a weak amplitude model naturally gets little weight.

Ledoit-Wolf currently shrinks each subject's noisy short-scan correlation toward the identity. That target is biologically implausible and pulls every subject away from the reference point used for the tangent embedding. This change keeps the same analytic, data-driven LW shrinkage strength per subject, but shrinks toward the training-fold population mean correlation instead, as in the PoSCE approach (Rahim et al. 2019). Short, noisy scans then fall back toward the group prior, and the remaining deviations are less dominated by sampling noise. The intensity is computed only over valid (in-FOV) ROI pairs. Out-of-FOV ROIs are still filled in from the same population matrix.

The Athena time series still contain the global signal. Global fluctuations from motion, respiration, arousal and scanner differences push every connection up together, so they dominate the tangent-space deviations and can mask the regional ADHD connectivity signal. This round I regress the mean signal of the in-FOV ROIs out of each subject's time series before the Ledoit-Wolf correlation; dead ROIs are left untouched, so the existing fill-in still works. Everything after that is unchanged.

Global signal regression helped only slightly (+0.0012), and whether to apply it is still debated. GSR removes physiological and motion noise, but it can also remove real global signal and create anticorrelations. The GSR and non-GSR connectomes therefore probably make partly different errors. This round I run the current tangent-space + LR pipeline once on each version of the same CC200 data and average their logits. Each pipeline gets its own training-fold fill-in for out-of-field-of-view ROIs, its own reference and its own scaling. Averaging should cut the variance of the weak ADHD signal without adding atlases, which hurt in round 3.

ADHD children move more, and the provided time series only had motion regression, which leaves short motion and physiological spikes in. Those spikes inflate correlations across the whole brain and add noise to the tangent-space deviations. This round I estimate DVARS from each subject's ROI signals (no labels used) and drop outlier frames, plus one frame before and two after each, before GSR and the Ledoit-Wolf correlation. At most 30% of a subject's frames are dropped. The rest of the pipeline is unchanged.

ADHD connectivity effects are thought to be network-level (for example DMN versus task-positive, fronto-striatal and cerebellar). Plain L2 on about 20k individual tangent edges can't pool the weak, consistent effects spread across many edges of the same network pair. This round I cluster the CC200 ROIs into 17 functional networks, using spectral clustering of the training-fold population correlation (no labels). I then append each network-pair's sum of tangent coordinates as extra features. Under the same L2 penalty this is exactly a hierarchical prior where edge weights = individual + shared network-pair weight, which raises SNR for distributed effects and leaves edge-level detail available.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in protocol and population (eyes open vs closed, age ranges, scanners), so the connectivity pattern that best separates ADHD from controls probably differs somewhat between sites. This round I keep the shared L2 logistic regression and add a per-site copy of the features (multi-task "frustratingly easy" domain adaptation). Each subject's weights become a shared vector plus a smaller site-specific vector, so subjects from the same site count about 1.5× as similar as subjects from different sites. To keep this cheap, I use the representer theorem: projecting the features onto the n-dimensional span of the training subjects gives the same L2-LR solution. Site is used only to decide which copy a subject's features go into, which helps within-site discrimination; it is never a predictor on its own.

ADHD prevalence differs a lot between ADHD-200 sites, so right now the penalized connectivity weights (shared and site-specific) are partly used up fitting each site's case rate through site-mean directions in tangent space. Within-site AUROC can't reward that. This round I add a near-unpenalized per-site intercept (site one-hot columns scaled ×10) that absorbs base-rate differences during training, so the L2 budget goes to within-site connectivity differences. At test time it only adds a constant per site, which cannot change within-site rankings.

The harness scores AUROC within each site, but the logistic loss also rewards separating subjects from different sites, for example sites whose ADHD rates differ. This round I replace the pointwise logistic loss with a pairwise logistic loss over (ADHD, control) pairs from the same site only, which is a direct surrogate for within-site AUROC. Rounds 7 and 19 only reweighted the pointwise loss or gave each site its own intercept, which is not the same thing. The features, the shared plus site-specific weights and the L2 penalty stay the same, and each site's pair loss is scaled so its gradient at zero matches the logistic regression's. That keeps C=0.001 comparable.
